claim: The carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase (Pol) II in mammals consists of 52 conserved heptapeptide repeats containing the consensus sequence Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7.
source: In mammals, the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase (Pol) II consists of 52 conserved heptapeptide repeats containing the consensus sequence Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual description of the CTD structure.

claim: Post-translational modifications of the CTD coordinate the transcription cycle and various steps of mRNA maturation.
source: Post-translational modifications of the CTD coordinate the transcription cycle and various steps of mRNA maturation.
evidence: This is a general statement about CTD function presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation (Tyr1P) is a hallmark of promoter (5′ associated) Pol II in mammalian cells.
source: Here we describe Tyr1 phosphorylation (Tyr1P) as a hallmark of promoter (5′ associated) Pol II in mammalian cells, in contrast to what was described in yeast.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ChIP-seq data showing Tyr1P predominantly at promoters.

claim: Tyr1P localization in mammalian cells contrasts with what was described in yeast.
source: Here we describe Tyr1 phosphorylation (Tyr1P) as a hallmark of promoter (5′ associated) Pol II in mammalian cells, in contrast to what was described in yeast.
evidence: This comparison is explicitly stated and references prior work on yeast.

claim: Tyr1P is predominantly found in antisense orientation at promoters.
source: Tyr1P is predominantly found in antisense orientation at promoters but is also specifically enriched at active enhancers.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by ChIP-seq data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Tyr1P is specifically enriched at active enhancers.
source: Tyr1P is predominantly found in antisense orientation at promoters but is also specifically enriched at active enhancers.
evidence: This finding is supported by ChIP-seq data at enhancer regions shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutation of Tyr1 to phenylalanine (Y1F) prevents the formation of the hyper-phosphorylated Pol IIO form.
source: Mutation of Tyr1 to phenylalanine (Y1F) prevents the formation of the hyper-phosphorylated Pol IIO form, induces degradation of Pol II to the truncated Pol IIB form, and results in a lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Y1F mutation induces degradation of Pol II to the truncated Pol IIB form.
source: Mutation of Tyr1 to phenylalanine (Y1F) prevents the formation of the hyper-phosphorylated Pol IIO form, induces degradation of Pol II to the truncated Pol IIB form, and results in a lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is observed in western blot experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Y1F mutation results in a lethal phenotype.
source: Mutation of Tyr1 to phenylalanine (Y1F) prevents the formation of the hyper-phosphorylated Pol IIO form, induces degradation of Pol II to the truncated Pol IIB form, and results in a lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability experiments after α-amanitin treatment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tyr1P has evolved specialized and essential functions in higher eukaryotes associated with antisense promoter and enhancer transcription.
source: Our results suggest that Tyr1P has evolved specialized and essential functions in higher eukaryotes associated with antisense promoter and enhancer transcription, and Pol II stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing differential localization in mammals vs. yeast and the lethal phenotype of Y1F mutation.

claim: Tyr1P is associated with Pol II stability.
source: Our results suggest that Tyr1P has evolved specialized and essential functions in higher eukaryotes associated with antisense promoter and enhancer transcription, and Pol II stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the degradation of Pol II observed in Y1F mutants.

claim: Ser5P and Ser2P are well-known CTD modifications associated with early transcription and elongation, respectively.
source: In the recent years, novel PTMs were described in addition to the well-known Ser5P and Ser2P associated with early transcription and elongation, respectively.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ser7P is involved in snRNA gene transcription.
source: These include Ser7P, involved in snRNA gene transcription (Chapman et al., 2007; Egloff et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Thr4P is associated with transcription elongation in mammals.
source: Thr4P associated to transcription elongation in mammals (Hintermair et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Thr4P is associated with histone gene transcription in chicken.
source: and to histone gene transcription in chicken (Hsin et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In yeast, Tyr1P is found at gene body locations, consistent with a role in transcription elongation.
source: and Tyr1P that in yeast is found at gene body locations, consistent with a role in transcription elongation (Mayer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and contrasts with the mammalian findings.

claim: Tyr1P was detected in western blots for all examined mouse and human cell lines.
source: We investigated various mouse and human cells and could detect Tyr1P in western blots for all examined lines, in most cases associated with the hyper-phosphorylated IIO form of Pol II (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tyr1P is in most cases associated with the hyper-phosphorylated IIO form of Pol II.
source: We investigated various mouse and human cells and could detect Tyr1P in western blots for all examined lines, in most cases associated with the hyper-phosphorylated IIO form of Pol II (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Y1F mutation was generated in CTD repeats 4 to 51.
source: we next generated Raji cell lines expressing Pol II resistant to α-amanitin (Chapman et al., 2004) and carrying either wild-type (WT) or a mutant Rpb1 gene with substitution of tyrosine to phenylalanine (Y1F) in CTD repeats 4 to 51 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Y1F phenotype is more drastic than T4A or S7A mutations.
source: This phenotype reveals an essential function of the Y1 residue that appears more drastic than T4A or S7A mutations, but comparable with that of S5A (Chapman et al., 2007; Hintermair et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made based on the observed lethal phenotype and cited prior work.

claim: The Y1F phenotype is comparable with that of S5A mutation.
source: This phenotype reveals an essential function of the Y1 residue that appears more drastic than T4A or S7A mutations, but comparable with that of S5A (Chapman et al., 2007; Hintermair et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made based on the observed lethal phenotype and cited prior work.

claim: Tyr1P very likely contributes to stabilization of CTD.
source: We conclude that Tyr1P very likely contributes to stabilization of CTD and may occur early within the transcription cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the degradation observed in Y1F mutants.

claim: Tyr1P may occur early within the transcription cycle.
source: We conclude that Tyr1P very likely contributes to stabilization of CTD and may occur early within the transcription cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data showing association with Ser5P and Ser7P.

claim: Tyr1P co-immunoprecipitated with Ser5P and Ser7P but not Ser2P or Thr4P.
source: Our experiments indicated clearly that Tyr1P co-immunoprecipitated with Ser5P and Ser7P but not Ser2P or Thr4P (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Signals for Tyr1P were observed in Ser5P and Ser7P but not in Ser2P co-immunoprecipitations.
source: Consistently, signals for Tyr1P were observed in Ser5P and Ser7P but not in Ser2P co-immunoprecipitations.
evidence: This is shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A.

claim: Tyr1P is associated with early transcribing isoforms of human Pol II.
source: Thus, overall, this data points out an association of Tyr1P with early transcribing isoforms of human Pol II.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Tyr1P signal is predominantly found at promoters similarly to Ser5P.
source: Our profiling analysis shows that Tyr1P signal is predominantly found at promoters similarly to Ser5P, weak or essentially absent at gene bodies and weak at 3′ends in contrast to Ser2P elongating mark and Ser7P (associated to both promoters and gene bodies).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide profiling shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tyr1P is weak or essentially absent at gene bodies.
source: Our profiling analysis shows that Tyr1P signal is predominantly found at promoters similarly to Ser5P, weak or essentially absent at gene bodies and weak at 3′ends in contrast to Ser2P elongating mark and Ser7P (associated to both promoters and gene bodies).
evidence: This is shown by genome-wide profiling in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Tyr1P is weak at 3′ ends of genes.
source: Our profiling analysis shows that Tyr1P signal is predominantly found at promoters similarly to Ser5P, weak or essentially absent at gene bodies and weak at 3′ends in contrast to Ser2P elongating mark and Ser7P (associated to both promoters and gene bodies).
evidence: This is shown by genome-wide profiling in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Human Tyr1P is mainly associated to promoters in an early, post-initiation step of transcription.
source: These observations are further supported by quantification of signals at various genic sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and reinforce our conclusion that human Tyr1P is mainly associated to promoters in an early, post-initiation step of transcription.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by ChIP-seq profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Chicken Tyr1 is found phosphorylated in the nucleoplasm.
source: Although we did not further investigate this possibility, in the accompanying manuscript, Hsin et al show that Chicken Tyr1 is found phosphorylated in the nucleoplasm, raising the possibility that Tyr1P is also associated with recruitment of the enzyme and transcription initiation.
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript by Hsin et al.

claim: Tyr1P might be associated with recruitment of the enzyme and transcription initiation.
source: Although we did not further investigate this possibility, in the accompanying manuscript, Hsin et al show that Chicken Tyr1 is found phosphorylated in the nucleoplasm, raising the possibility that Tyr1P is also associated with recruitment of the enzyme and transcription initiation.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility raised based on findings in chicken.

claim: Genomic profiling at the vicinity of the TSS indicates two main peaks of Pol II upstream and downstream of the TSS.
source: Genomic profiling at the vicinity of the transcription start site (TSS) indicates two main peaks of Pol II upstream and downstream of the TSS (Figure 2D, left panel and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq profiling data in Figure 2D.

claim: The two Pol II peaks at TSS most likely reflect sense and antisense paused transcription.
source: These peaks most likely reflect sense and antisense paused transcription as evidenced by our short strand specific (ssRNA) sequencing analysis, as previously described (Core et al., 2008; Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008; Fenouil et al., 2012) for mammalian promoters.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by ssRNA-seq data and cited prior work.

claim: Tyr1P showed a clearly distinct pattern with a more pronounced upstream peak compared to Ser5P and Ser7P.
source: By comparing the signals of these two peaks with that of the Ser5P and Ser7P isoforms, Tyr1P showed a clearly distinct pattern with a more pronounced upstream peak (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and examples in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiling shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The antisense/sense (AS/S) difference was significant for Tyr1P as compared to other isoforms.
source: We confirmed this result with an independent Tyr1P antibody (8G5) harboring wider range of CTD peptide recognition (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), and by using statistical analysis showing that antisense/sense (AS/S) difference was significant for Tyr1P as compared to other isoforms (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E with p-values.

claim: Tyr1P is predominantly associated with upstream polymerases, mostly reflecting AS transcription at mammalian promoters.
source: Together, our analyses indicate that Tyr1P is predominantly associated with upstream polymerases, mostly reflecting AS transcription at mammalian promoters.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChIP-seq profiling and statistical analyses.

claim: Mammalian promoters associated with Pol II can be grouped in three main classes in mouse T-lymphocytes.
source: We previously showed that mammalian promoters associated with Pol II can be grouped in three main classes in mouse T-lymphocytes (Fenouil et al., 2012), based on ranking of the main Pol II signal from the most upstream to the most downstream of the TSS.
evidence: This is cited from prior work by the authors.

claim: The three classes of promoters were reproduced in human Raji B-cells by ranking the signal of Tyr1P.
source: We reproduced this result and the main features of the three groups in human Raji B-cells by ranking the signal of Tyr1P (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The first class of promoters harbors strongly paused Pol II at promoters with high GC content and CpG islands.
source: The first class (the majority of genes), with Pol II signals most upstream of TSSs, harbors strongly paused Pol II at promoters with high GC content and CpG islands (CGIs) and is associated with the highest level of bidirectional and AS transcription.
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first class of promoters is associated with the highest level of bidirectional and AS transcription.
source: The first class (the majority of genes), with Pol II signals most upstream of TSSs, harbors strongly paused Pol II at promoters with high GC content and CpG islands (CGIs) and is associated with the highest level of bidirectional and AS transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ssRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The second class of promoters has a sharper Pol II peak centered close to the TSS and lower GC content.
source: The second class, with a sharper Pol II peak centered close to the TSS and lower GC content, contains mostly mono-directional sense paused transcription
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second class of promoters contains mostly mono-directional sense paused transcription.
source: The second class, with a sharper Pol II peak centered close to the TSS and lower GC content, contains mostly mono-directional sense paused transcription
evidence: This is demonstrated by ssRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The third class of promoters contains more downstream Pol II with less pause.
source: whereas the third class contains more downstream Pol II with less pause.
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In class I promoters, Tyr1P is essentially observed in AS while Ser5P, Ser7P, or total Pol II generally show a second peak around the TSS reflecting sense and bidirectional transcription.
source: In this class, Tyr1P is essentially observed in AS while Ser5P, Ser7P, or total Pol II generally show a second peak around the TSS reflecting sense and therefore bidirectional transcription (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by profiling data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In AS orientation, Tyr1P associates mainly with the leading edge of Pol II.
source: This indicates that AS Tyr1P relates to one specific class of promoters and suggests that in AS orientation, Tyr1P associates mainly with the leading edge of Pol II.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial positioning analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The location of the AS Tyr1P in class I is found more downstream on average as compared to Pol II or Ser5P.
source: Pleading for this hypothesis, the location of the AS Tyr1P in class I is found more downstream on average as compared to Pol II or Ser5P, and locates just after the −2 nucleosome midpoint (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the profiling data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: AS Tyr1P locates just after the −2 nucleosome midpoint.
source: Pleading for this hypothesis, the location of the AS Tyr1P in class I is found more downstream on average as compared to Pol II or Ser5P, and locates just after the −2 nucleosome midpoint (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown by the nucleosome positioning data in Figure 3B,C.

claim: For the majority of promoters significantly associated with AS short RNAs in class I, Tyr1P is either located at the immediate proximity or after the main Pol II peak.
source: A more detailed investigation of the individual positions of phospho-isoforms further shows that for the majority of promoters significantly associated with AS short RNAs in class I, Tyr1P is either located at the immediate proximity or after the main Pol II peak (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spatial analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tyr1P might play a role in early elongation.
source: A more detailed investigation of the individual positions of phospho-isoforms further shows that for the majority of promoters significantly associated with AS short RNAs in class I, Tyr1P is either located at the immediate proximity or after the main Pol II peak (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) suggesting that it might play a role in early elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the spatial positioning data.

claim: Ser7 mutations do not show significant phenotype.
source: Although Ser7P displayed similar characteristics, its influence on transcription of coding genes is likely to be minor, as Ser7 mutations do not show significant phenotype (Chapman et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Ser7 mutations do not show transcriptome impairment.
source: or transcriptome impairment (JCA and DE, unpublished observations).
evidence: This is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: Tyr1P is a CTD PTM that associates with the 5′ end of genes and shows a stronger linkage to paused Pol II at promoters with bidirectional and AS transcription.
source: We overall conclude that Tyr1P is a CTD PTM that associates with the 5′ end of genes and shows a stronger linkage to paused Pol II at promoters with bidirectional and AS transcription.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq and ssRNA-seq data.

claim: Highly active and tissue-specific enhancers are transcribed by Pol II in various tissues.
source: Many groups including ours have shown that highly active and tissue-specific enhancers are transcribed by Pol II in various tissues (De Santa et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2010; Koch et al., 2011; Natoli and Andrau, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: Active enhancers can be hallmarked by the occurrence of H3K4me1high/H3K4me3low epigenetic marks combination.
source: These enhancers can also be hallmarked by the occurrence of H3K4me1high/H3K4me3low epigenetic marks combination (Koch et al., 2011; Pekowska et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: 390 B-cell enhancers were isolated using stringent criteria.
source: Using these criteria, we isolated 390 B-cells enhancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The isolated enhancers were associated with genes specific to B-cells.
source: Our selection was further validated using tissue-specificity analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) indicating IGRs associated with genes specific to B-cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue specificity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The isolated enhancers were associated with Ser5P.
source: As before (Koch et al., 2011), we observed that these IGRs were associated with Ser5P (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq profiling in Figure 4A.

claim: The isolated enhancers were not associated with Ser2P Pol II.
source: but not with Ser2P Pol II (not shown)
evidence: This is stated based on ChIP-seq data.

claim: The isolated enhancers were associated with short transcripts reflecting paused transcription.
source: as well as with short transcripts (reflecting paused transcription) and a discrete nucleosome depleted region.
evidence: This is shown by ssRNA-seq and MNase-seq data in Figure 4A.

claim: The isolated enhancers were associated with a discrete nucleosome depleted region.
source: as well as with short transcripts (reflecting paused transcription) and a discrete nucleosome depleted region.
evidence: This is shown by MNase-seq data in Figure 4A.

claim: Signal for both Ser7P and Tyr1P was found at enhancers.
source: Consistent with early elongating Pol II at enhancers, we found signal for both Ser7P and Tyr1P at these IGRs.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 4A.

claim: Tyr1P appeared more bound to enhancers as compared to promoters and total Pol II.
source: Importantly, Tyr1P appeared more bound to enhancers as compared to promoters and total Pol II (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tyr1 is more phosphorylated than Ser5 or Ser7 at enhancers.
source: suggesting that Tyr1 is more phosphorylated than Ser5 or Ser7 at enhancers and represent a hallmark of these essential areas of the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the relative enrichment data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tyr1P represents a hallmark of enhancers.
source: suggesting that Tyr1 is more phosphorylated than Ser5 or Ser7 at enhancers and represent a hallmark of these essential areas of the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enrichment data.

claim: Tyr1P displayed the best correlation with Pol II at isolated enhancers.
source: Additionally, Tyr1P also displayed the best correlation with Pol II at isolated enhancers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown by Spearman correlation analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: An independent selection for active enhancers based on H3K27ac brought very similar results.
source: Finally, using an independent selection for active enhancers based on H3K27ac brought very similar results (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tyr1P is a strong signature of Pol II-transcribed active enhancers associated with tissue-specific gene expression.
source: Together, our investigations showed that Tyr1P is a strong signature of Pol II-transcribed active enhancers associated with tissue-specific gene expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChIP-seq and tissue specificity analyses.

claim: Tyr1P associates with 5′ Pol II and AS transcription at promoters.
source: Here, we described that Tyr1P associates with 5′ Pol II and AS transcription at promoters and is a signature of active, tissue-specific enhancers in human B-cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Tyr1P is a signature of active, tissue-specific enhancers in human B-cells.
source: Here, we described that Tyr1P associates with 5′ Pol II and AS transcription at promoters and is a signature of active, tissue-specific enhancers in human B-cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by ChIP-seq and tissue specificity data.

claim: The findings regarding Tyr1P in mammals contrast with features of Tyr1P in yeast.
source: These findings contrast with features of Tyr1P in yeast, which is located at gene bodies and proposed to play a role in elongation by impairing termination factor recruitment (Mayer et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made with cited prior work on yeast.

claim: In yeast, Tyr1P is located at gene bodies and proposed to play a role in elongation by impairing termination factor recruitment.
source: These findings contrast with features of Tyr1P in yeast, which is located at gene bodies and proposed to play a role in elongation by impairing termination factor recruitment (Mayer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: A conserved PTM has evolved to display specialized functions specific to metazoans.
source: These apparent discrepancies thus provide an interesting paradigm whereby a conserved PTM has evolved to display specialized functions specific to metazoans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: S. cerevisiae genes are very compact, mostly devoid of introns.
source: However, S. cerevisiae genes are very compact, mostly devoid of introns and promoters structure is also extremely divergent in both length and sequence between yeast (around 100–200 nt, AT-rich) and mammals (around 1000 nt, GC-rich).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about yeast genome structure.

claim: Yeast promoters are around 100–200 nt and AT-rich.
source: However, S. cerevisiae genes are very compact, mostly devoid of introns and promoters structure is also extremely divergent in both length and sequence between yeast (around 100–200 nt, AT-rich) and mammals (around 1000 nt, GC-rich).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about yeast promoter structure.

claim: Mammalian promoters are around 1000 nt and GC-rich.
source: However, S. cerevisiae genes are very compact, mostly devoid of introns and promoters structure is also extremely divergent in both length and sequence between yeast (around 100–200 nt, AT-rich) and mammals (around 1000 nt, GC-rich).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian promoter structure.

claim: Enhancers do not exist per se in yeast.
source: Furthermore, enhancers do not exist per se in yeast.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about yeast genome organization.

claim: Hsin et al. describe similar observations regarding stability of Y1F mutant in chicken cells.
source: In an accompanying manuscript, Hsin et al. (2014) describe similar observations regarding stability of Y1F mutant in chicken cells and involvement of Tyr1P in AS transcription at promoters
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript.

claim: Hsin et al. describe involvement of Tyr1P in AS transcription at promoters in chicken.
source: In an accompanying manuscript, Hsin et al. (2014) describe similar observations regarding stability of Y1F mutant in chicken cells and involvement of Tyr1P in AS transcription at promoters
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript.

claim: The observations regarding Tyr1P are conserved in vertebrates.
source: thus providing further evidence that our observations are conserved in vertebrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar findings in chicken.

claim: Differential CTD PTMs might play a role in regulating the directionality of transcription.
source: We therefore speculate that differential CTD PTMs might not only reflect, but also play a role in regulating the directionality of transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Tyr1P might be involved in a transcriptional state marking the transition between early and productive elongation.
source: Based on the spatial location of Tyr1P in class I promoters, mostly found at the leading edge of Pol II in opposite orientation of the gene, it is tempting to speculate that this PTM might be involved in a transcriptional state marking the transition between early and productive elongation, providing a checkpoint for transcriptional complexes to proceed in productive elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the spatial positioning data.

claim: Tyr1P might provide a checkpoint for transcriptional complexes to proceed in productive elongation.
source: Based on the spatial location of Tyr1P in class I promoters, mostly found at the leading edge of Pol II in opposite orientation of the gene, it is tempting to speculate that this PTM might be involved in a transcriptional state marking the transition between early and productive elongation, providing a checkpoint for transcriptional complexes to proceed in productive elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Pol II might become competent for elongation as well as for overcoming the nucleosomal barrier both in sense and antisense orientation depending on the level of Tyr1P at promoters.
source: Depending on the level of Tyr1P at promoters, Pol II might become competent for elongation as well as for overcoming the nucleosomal barrier both in sense and antisense orientation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Less Pol II molecules are able to effectively enter elongation in AS orientation.
source: Since less Pol II molecules are able to effectively enter elongation in AS orientation, more accumulation of the Tyr1P could be observed upstream of the TSS toward the leading edge of Pol II.
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric distribution of Tyr1P and ssRNA data.

claim: Degradation of Y1F mutant is due to absence of Tyr1P checkpoint signal.
source: This could also explain degradation of Y1F mutant that is due to absence of Tyr1P checkpoint signal, would accumulate around the edge of the promoters and become degraded.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed degradation.

claim: There could be a link between hyperphosphorylation of Tyr1 in AS orientation and exosome machinery recruitment to degrade nascent RNA prior release of the Pol II enzyme.
source: Finally there could also be a link between hyperphosphorylation of Tyr1 in AS orientation and exosome machinery recruitment to degrade nascent RNA prior release of the Pol II enzyme (Preker et al., 2008; Andersen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: Pol II and all isoforms, including Tyr1P, correlated with transcription levels of genes.
source: We isolated significantly associated regions based on the signal distribution of the background-subtracted data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and found that Pol II and all isoforms, including Tyr1P, correlated with transcription levels of genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation with microarray expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At many gene locations, a predominant signal of Tyr1P at promoters was observed.
source: At many gene locations, a predominant signal of Tyr1P at promoters was observed (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq examples in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Raji cells were transfected with wild-type and Y1F Rpb1 expression vectors by electroporation.
source: Cells were transfected with the wild-type and (Y1F) Rpb1 expression vectors by electroporation (10 μg of plasmid DNA/107 cells; 960 μF, 250 V).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: ChIP-seq experiments were performed essentially as described before using same standard and QC.
source: ChIP-seq and MNase-seq experiments were performed essentially as described before using same standard and QC for experiments (Fenouil et al., 2012).
evidence: This references the methods used with citation to prior work.
